questions.prompt: Why can the optimal action in a state depend on the number of steps remaining?
options: Immediate reward and future payoff trade off differently with different remaining time
The discount factor is drawn at random at each step, so the value of a state varies
The state itself changes as steps pass, so the same action is evaluated in a new place
The transition probabilities drift with time, so the model used for planning is different at each step
questions.explanation: With one step left only immediate reward counts; with more steps, future payoff can dominate.

questions.prompt: V_0=0. State B: work pays 3 and stays in B. Optimal value V_3(B)?
Walk succeeds with probability p=0.5 (else stays in A, reward 0), V_1(B)=3, V_1(A)=1. Value of walking in A with 2 steps to go?
A fixed open-loop plan is compared with a closed-loop policy on a stochastic system. Which is always true?
options: The open-loop plan is better because it is simpler
The closed-loop optimum is at least as good as every open-loop plan
The closed-loop optimum is worse because it needs sensing
questions.explanation: An open-loop plan is a special policy that ignores feedback.

questions.prompt: Belief (A=1). Walk: A stays with 0.2, B 0.8. Sensor: P('a'|A)=0.9, P('a'|B)=0.1. Posterior P(A) after seeing 'a'? (3 decimals)
An open-loop plan succeeds only if a 0.8-probability step succeeds; then it earns 9, else 0. Expected return?
A robot reads a noisy sensor and always treats the last reading as the true state. The main risk is:
options: Violating the Markov property of the sensor, which makes any filtering approach invalid
Planning over a longer horizon, because stale readings accumulate over successive steps
Using too much memory, because the controller must store every past reading of the sensor
Acting confidently on an error; a belief would keep the uncertainty
questions.explanation: The last reading is wrong with probability related to the sensor error.

questions.prompt: Compare a greedy choice with a multi-step plan for a robot choosing between grabbing a nearby object and walking to a better station. State what you would compute, the horizon dependence and how you would check that planning helps.
rubric: Compute the expected return of both over the task horizon with backward induction.
Identify the horizon at which the preferred action switches.
Check against a greedy baseline and a brute-force enumeration of plans.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
